lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding the skills you already have
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your life and work experience into a list of job skills.
This lesson builds toward: Given your work, training, volunteer and life experience, inside or outside, you will list your job skills in employer words, with one true example each, keeping only skills that are true for you.
Most people have more skills than they think. Work in a prison kitchen, laundry or maintenance shop, military service, caring for a family member, church volunteering, cutting hair or fixing cars for neighbors: all of it builds skills employers want.
Ask an AI assistant to help you name them: "I worked 3 years in a large kitchen preparing meals for 500 people a day and trained new workers. What job skills does that show? Use words employers use." You might get: food safety, working under time pressure, training others, inventory, teamwork.
Make a master list of skills with one example each. Do not let AI add skills you do not really have. Everything on your résumé must be true, because you may be asked about it in the interview.
Step by step:
- List every job, training, volunteer role and responsibility you have had, inside or outside.
- For each, ask AI what skills it shows, in employer words.
- Keep only skills that are true for you.
- Write one real example for each skill.
Words to know:
- Transferable skill: a skill from one setting that is useful in another.
- Soft skill: a people skill like teamwork, reliability or communication.
- Hard skill: a specific ability like forklift driving, cooking or using Excel.
Try it now: Describe three things you have done to an AI assistant and ask what job skills they show. Write a master list of at least eight true skills, each with one example.
You can now turn your experience into a true list of job skills in employer language.

options: A skill you can only use in one job
A skill from one setting that is useful in another
A skill you pay to learn
check.why: Transferable skills, like training others, move from one setting to another.

check.q: You fixed cars for neighbors for years with no paycheck. What do you do with that experience?
options: Leave it out; it was not a real job
Say you were a licensed mechanic
Wait until an interviewer asks about it
Ask AI what skills it shows and list the true ones with an example
check.why: Informal work builds real skills; list only the ones that are true, with an example.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing a one-page résumé with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a clean, one-page résumé tailored to a real job post.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real job post and a free template, you will create a one-page résumé tailored to the job, with action-word bullets and numbers, with every word true and no Social Security number, date of birth or photo.
A résumé is a one-page summary of your skills, experience and training. A simple layout works best: name and contact, a two-line summary, skills, experience, and education or training. Use a free template in Google Docs or Microsoft Word.
Tailor it to each job. Paste the job post (not your private details) into the AI and ask: "Which skills and keywords does this job want? Which of my skills match?" Then ask it to write bullet points from your examples that start with action words and include numbers: "Prepared meals for 500 people daily while meeting food safety standards."
For work done while incarcerated, you can list the facility type or employer the way your reentry counselor suggests, such as the state department of corrections, and focus on the skills. Never put your Social Security number, date of birth or a photo on a U.S. résumé.
Step by step:
- Open a free résumé template in Google Docs or Word.
- Paste the job post into AI and ask which keywords it wants.
- Ask AI to write action-word bullets from your true examples, with numbers.
- Fill in the template and keep it to one page.
- Check every word for truth and spelling.
Words to know:
- Résumé: a one-page summary of your skills, experience and training.
- Keyword: an important word from the job post that employers and software look for.
- Tailor: change your résumé to fit a specific job.
Try it now: Find one real job post. Use AI to find its keywords and write five bullet points from your true examples. Put them into a one-page résumé template.
You can now build a one-page résumé tailored to a real job post with AI help.

check.q: What should you paste into AI to tailor your résumé?
check.why: Paste the job post, not your private details, so AI can find the keywords.

check.q: Your résumé is a page and a half for an entry-level job. What do you do?
options: Cut it to the strongest bullets that match the job, on one page
check.why: Most entry-level résumés should fit on one page, focused on what the job wants.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing a short cover letter
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a cover letter under 200 words that sounds like you.
This lesson builds toward: For the same job post, you will write a cover letter in three short paragraphs, under 200 words and sounding like you when read out loud.
A cover letter is a short letter that says why you want this job and why you are a good fit. Many jobs do not require one, but a good one can set you apart.
Use three short paragraphs: why this job and company, two skills that match what they need with a quick example, and a thank-you with how to reach you. Ask AI: "Write a cover letter under 200 words for this job post using these two skills and examples. Friendly, confident, simple words."
Then make it yours. Change any phrase you would never say. Add one true detail about why you want to work there. Read it out loud: if it does not sound like you, change it again.
Step by step:
- Paragraph 1: why this job and company.
- Paragraph 2: two matching skills with examples.
- Paragraph 3: thanks and how to reach you.
- Ask AI to draft it under 200 words.
- Edit it to sound like you, and read it out loud.
Words to know:
- Cover letter: a short letter sent with a résumé explaining why you fit the job.
Try it now: Write a cover letter for your job post with AI, keep it under 200 words, and edit it until it sounds like you when you read it out loud.
You can now write a short, personal cover letter with AI help.

check.q: What goes in the second paragraph of the cover letter?
options: Two skills that match the job, with a quick example
check.why: Paragraph 2 gives two matching skills with examples.

check.q: AI's cover letter says "I am exceedingly enthusiastic to leverage my synergies." What do you do?
options: Change it to words you would really say
check.why: Change any phrase you would never say so the letter sounds like you.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Interviews and the job search

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Practicing interviews with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI as a practice interviewer and improve your answers.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant as a practice interviewer, you will answer five common interview questions out loud, using STAR for "tell me about a time" questions, without reading from notes.
AI can act as an interviewer. Ask: "You are hiring for this job [paste job post]. Ask me one interview question at a time. After I answer, give me one thing I did well and one thing to improve." Many AI apps let you talk out loud, which is great practice.
Use the STAR method for "tell me about a time" questions: Situation, Task, Action, Result. "In the kitchen (situation) we had to serve 500 meals in an hour (task). I set up a prep line and trained two new workers (action). We finished on time every day that month (result)."
Prepare five common questions: tell me about yourself, why do you want this job, a strength, a time you solved a problem, and do you have any questions for us. Practice until you can answer without reading.
Step by step:
- Paste the job post and ask AI to interview you one question at a time.
- Answer out loud or by typing.
- Use STAR for "tell me about a time" questions.
- Ask for one strength and one improvement after each answer.
- Practice five questions until you do not need notes.
Words to know:
- STAR method: a way to answer: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
- Mock interview: a practice interview.
Try it now: Run a mock interview with AI for your job post. Answer five questions out loud using STAR where it fits, and write down the feedback.
You can now practice interviews with AI and answer with the STAR method.

check.q: In the STAR method, what does "Result" mean?
options: What happened because of what you did
check.why: Result is the outcome of your action, like finishing on time every day.

check.q: You can only answer "Tell me about yourself" by reading your notes. What do you do?
options: Practice it out loud with AI until you can answer without notes
Skip that question in the interview
Memorize a long speech AI wrote
Bring the notes and read them
check.why: Practice out loud until you can answer without reading.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Talking about gaps or a record with confidence
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Prepare a short, honest, forward-looking answer about a gap or background.
This lesson builds toward: If you have a gap or a record, you will prepare a short, honest answer that turns to why you are ready now, using only facts you are comfortable sharing, said calmly out loud.
Gaps happen: prison, illness, caregiving, military moves, layoffs. Employers mostly want to know you are ready now. Prepare a short answer: be honest, keep it brief, show what you learned or did, and turn to why you are ready for this job.
Example: "I made a mistake and served time. While there I earned my food handler certificate and ran the kitchen line. I'm ready to bring that work ethic here." Ask AI to help you shorten and steady your answer, but use only facts you are comfortable sharing, and leave out case numbers and details.
Know your supports. Many U.S. states and cities have fair chance or "ban the box" rules about when employers can ask about records; check your state labor department or a reentry legal aid group. The Federal Bonding Program offers free fidelity bonds to employers who hire at-risk job seekers, covering the first six months. Some employers may also qualify for the Work Opportunity Tax Credit; check the IRS WOTC page for its current status and groups.
Step by step:
- Write the honest fact in one sentence.
- Add what you learned or did since.
- Add why you are ready for this job.
- Ask AI to make it shorter and steadier.
- Practice it out loud until it feels calm.
Words to know:
- Fair chance hiring: rules or practices that give people with records a fair look before asking about their past.
- Fidelity bond: insurance that protects an employer against loss from an employee's dishonesty.
Official sources:
- The Federal Bonding Program
- U.S. Department of Labor: Work Opportunity Tax Credit
- IRS: Work Opportunity Tax Credit
Try it now: Write a three-sentence answer about a gap or background (yours, or a practice one). Use AI to tighten it, then say it out loud three times.
You can now answer questions about a gap or record honestly and confidently, and name supports that can help.

check.q: What do employers mostly want to know when they ask about a gap?
options: That you are ready to work now
check.why: Employers mostly want to know you are ready now, so keep it brief and forward-looking.

check.q: An interviewer asks about your record. Which answer is best?
options: A long story with every detail
"I made a mistake and served time. I earned my food handler certificate there, and I'm ready to work."
check.why: Honest, brief and focused on what you learned and why you are ready.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Searching and applying safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find real job openings, track applications and avoid job scams.
This lesson builds toward: When you search and apply for jobs, you will find openings on trusted sites, track each application and check every post for scam warning signs, giving no bank or Social Security number before a real offer.
Look for jobs on trusted sites, company websites and at your local American Job Center, which offers free help with job search and training. Your reentry program, veterans office or workforce program may have job leads and employers who hire people with records.
Track every application in a simple sheet: company, job, date applied, contact, follow-up date. Follow up about a week later with a short, polite email. AI can draft it.
Watch for job scams. The FTC warns: honest employers do not charge you to get a job; be wary of big pay for little work, being asked to deposit a check and send money back, reshipping packages, or paying for training or certificates up front. Never give a bank account or Social Security number before you have a real offer from a real company. Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Step by step:
- Search trusted sites, company pages and your American Job Center.
- Track each application in a sheet.
- Follow up about a week later.
- Check each post for scam warning signs.
- Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- American Job Center: a free U.S. government-funded office that helps with job search and training.
- Job scam: a fake job offer meant to steal money or information.
Official sources:
- FTC: Job scams
- CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor): find an American Job Center
Try it now: Final task: finalize your tailored résumé, cover letter and five practiced interview answers for your real job post. Check the post against the scam signs, add it to a tracking sheet, and apply or have it ready to send.
You can now build a job kit with AI, interview with confidence and apply safely.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Tailored résumé Longer than one page, not matched to the job, or includes private numbers. One page with the job's keywords, action-word bullets with numbers, and no private numbers. Every bullet links to a skill the job post asks for. True skills A skill or claim on the résumé is not true. Every skill is true and backed by a real example. Skills from prison jobs, caregiving or informal work are described in employer words. Cover letter Over 200 words, or reads like a generic AI letter. Three short paragraphs under 200 words that sound like the learner. Includes one true detail about why they want to work there. Interview answers Fewer than five answers, or answers are read from notes. Five answers practiced out loud, with STAR for "tell me about a time". Uses AI feedback to improve at least two answers. Gap or background answer The answer is long, defensive or untrue (if it applies). Short, honest and ends with why the learner is ready now. Said calmly out loud without notes. Safe application The job post was not checked for scam signs. The post was checked against the scam signs and the application is tracked. A follow-up date is set for about a week later. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where can you get free help with a job search and training?
options: A website that charges a fee to apply
A text from an unknown number
A job that asks you to reship packages
check.why: American Job Centers offer free help with job search and training.

check.q: A "job" offers high pay for little work and asks for your bank account before any interview. What do you do?
options: Send only half the account number
Do not share it; check for scam signs and report it
check.why: Never give a bank account before a real offer; this has scam warning signs.
